summary: Petit-Rocher Lighthouse, first lit 24 May 1879 on Elm Tree Point and moved to the wharf end in 1910, now a Coast Guard skeleton tower at Petit-Rocher on Chaleur Bay.

light.note: First lit as a fixed white light (LighthouseFriends). Colour today disputed: red flash every 6 s (CCG List, Fl R 6s); yellow flash every 5 s (Lighthouse Directory). Flash 1 s, eclipse 5 s (CCG List).

structures.note: Original tower on Elm Tree Point, 9.4 m (LighthouseFriends); 9 m (30 ft) (Lighthouse Directory). Ended in a 1912 storm (LighthouseFriends) or demolition in 1929 (Lighthouse Directory). Sources disagree.

structures.type: square skeleton tower, red and white rectangular daymark
structures.note: At the outer end of the wharf. CCG List: 6.9 m structure height; Lighthouse Directory: 7 m (23 ft). Date of erection not in the sources read; the material is not given in the sources read.

structures.name: Petit-Rocher Breakwater Light
structures.type: pipe swing pole, green, white and black square daymark
structures.note: CCG List No. 1339.2: green, Fl G 6s, operates 24 hours. Seasonal.

staffing.note: Keepers to at least 1923 (LighthouseFriends). The date the light became automatic is not in the sources read. The CCG List marks the light seasonal.

access.note: Reached by walking the pier. Site open, tower closed.

events.note: Contract awarded to Joseph Morrison to erect a square wooden lighthouse on Elm Tree Point
Square wooden tower, 9.4 m (LighthouseFriends); total cost $952.60
Keeper Hilarion Roy first lit the fixed white light on 24 May 1879
A wharf built at Petit Rocher
Moved about 2.5 km south from the north side of the Elm Tree River mouth to the outer end of the wharf at Rochette (Church) Point

Original 9 m wooden tower demolished (Lighthouse Directory). Conflicts with the 1912 storm account; no source says the light was deactivated in 1929.

corrections.why: No source says the light was deactivated in 1929. The Lighthouse Directory says the original 9 m wooden tower was demolished that year, and the light is listed as active.

The CCG List gives a square skeleton tower 6.9 m high at the Petit-Rocher light now, and the Lighthouse Directory gives a 7 m square skeletal tower. The record's 1929 steel tower, marked lost, is probably the present tower; a human should confirm which one the record means.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 'sometimes inactive' note (Wikidata: deactivated 1929) is not supported. The Lighthouse Directory and the CCG List both show the light active today.

notes_for_editor: Most of the 1878 to 1912 history rests on LighthouseFriends alone. Its primary source is the Department's annual reports, but the local corpus starts in 1900, so the 1878 contract, the 1879 first light, the 1908 wharf, the 1910 move and the 1912 storm are not checked against a government report. The corpus shows the Department's keeper lists (1901 to 1907) with 'Boudreau, Jos. B Petit Rocher'; Roy is not in that range. The Department's 1913-14 works table has 'Petit Rocher ... Improvements to light and cutting down tower' against a column the OCR splits from its station list, so it is not used. The 1912 storm (LighthouseFriends) and the 1929 demolition (Lighthouse Directory) disagree about how the original tower ended; both are reported as sourced. Colour: the CCG List gives red (Fl R 6s), the Lighthouse Directory yellow (flash every 5 s); the record shows F R. Location: LighthouseFriends gives its page point as 47.783125, -65.707371, which sits at the village and not 2.5 km north of the wharf where LighthouseFriends places the 1879 site; the 1879 site is not located. Laplante: LighthouseFriends only; the Department's 1912 to 1916 keeper tables carry the name 'J. D. Laplante' but the OCR does not place him at Petit Rocher. Storms: the 1912 storm is LighthouseFriends' only mention. The place name appears as Petit-Rocher, Petit Rocher, Petit Rocher (Elmr Tree) and Rochette (Church) Point; the story uses Petit-Rocher. Photos: none added; the record's photo list is empty. The Lighthouse Directory calls the current structure a 7 m square skeletal tower; the CCG List gives 6.9 m; the record's 7.0 m steel tower is not in any source read.
